Family Health

Testicular cancer: diagnosis, treatment and fertility questions

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A change in a testicle deserves a medical assessment, even if it does not hurt. Many changes have a cause other than cancer, but an examination and the right tests are needed to tell. Testicular cancer is often very treatable, including in some advanced cases, and asking about future fertility early can help preserve options before treatment begins.

Where testicular cancer begins

The testicles sit in the scrotum, the skin pouch beneath the penis. They produce sperm and testosterone. Testicular cancer begins when cells in one of these organs become malignant; usually one testicle is affected, although both can be involved.

Most cases begin in germ cells, which are involved in making sperm. It is a cancer often diagnosed in younger adults, but neither a young nor an older age rules it out. A new lump or persistent change should not be dismissed because you fall outside a commonly quoted age range.

Seminoma, nonseminoma and less common tumors

The two main germ-cell groups are seminoma and nonseminoma. Seminomas generally grow and spread more slowly, while nonseminomas tend to progress faster. Either can spread beyond the testicle. A tumor containing both types is managed as a nonseminoma because that component affects treatment decisions.

Less common tumors arise in the supporting or hormone-producing tissue, called the stroma. Leydig-cell and Sertoli-cell tumors are examples. Many of these stromal tumors are benign, so the word tumor does not automatically mean cancer. The pathology report identifies the type and guides which treatment information applies to you.

Risk factors do not determine a diagnosis

An undescended testicle, also called cryptorchidism, is an important risk factor. This means a testicle did not move down into the scrotum as expected during development. A history of abnormal testicular development or a close relative with testicular cancer is also useful information to share with the clinician.

Rates differ across populations. For example, US data show higher rates in some White, American Indian and Alaska Native populations than in some other groups. This does not make ethnicity a diagnostic test or mean someone in a lower-rate group can ignore symptoms. Many people diagnosed with this cancer have no family history.

Changes to have checked, and pain that cannot wait

Possible changes include a lump, swelling, enlargement, a feeling of heaviness or firmness, or an ache in the testicle or scrotum. Some people notice discomfort in the lower abdomen or back. Others have few symptoms and a finding is picked up during an examination or another test.

Arrange prompt medical assessment for a new or persistent change. Symptoms alone cannot distinguish cancer from a cyst, infection or another cause. Sudden severe testicular pain, especially with nausea or vomiting, needs emergency assessment because a twisted testicle can lose its blood supply. Do not wait for a routine cancer appointment if that happens.

Examination, ultrasound and blood markers

The clinician asks about your symptoms and health history and examines the testicles and relevant lymph nodes. Ultrasound shows the internal structure and helps distinguish a solid mass from some noncancerous conditions. It provides information that a description or photograph of a lump cannot.

Blood tests may measure alpha-fetoprotein, or AFP, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin, or beta-hCG, and lactate dehydrogenase, or LDH. These tumor markers help with diagnosis, staging and later follow-up. Normal results do not exclude cancer, and an abnormal result needs interpretation alongside the scan and other findings. Pure seminoma does not normally raise AFP, which matters when deciding whether a nonseminoma component may be present.

Why surgery may be part of confirming the diagnosis

When the findings strongly suggest cancer, the usual operation removes the affected testicle through an incision in the groin. This is a radical inguinal orchiectomy. A pathologist examines the tissue to determine whether cancer is present and, if so, which type.

A routine needle or cutting biopsy through the scrotum is usually avoided when this cancer is suspected because it can alter the route of spread. That is different from saying all testicular biopsies are impossible or forbidden. Carefully selected situations may have a different specialist approach, including testis-sparing surgery; ask why the recommended procedure is appropriate in your case.

Stage describes more than where a lump is found

Scans, often including CT imaging, assess lymph nodes and other areas for spread. Pathology and blood-marker levels, including results after surgery, also contribute. Imaging may happen before or after the tissue diagnosis depending on the situation.

Broadly, stage I has no identified spread to distant sites or regional lymph nodes, though local tissue involvement and marker results create subgroups. Stage II involves regional lymph nodes, commonly at the back of the abdomen. Stage III can involve distant lymph nodes or organs such as the lungs, liver, bone or brain, but raised markers can also affect the stage even without distant spread.

For advanced germ-cell cancer, the team may also discuss good, intermediate or poor prognosis groups. These are different from stage numbers. The standard system does not have a poor-prognosis group for pure seminoma. Ask the team to explain both the stage and any risk group rather than interpreting one label by itself.

Surgery and surveillance are individualized

Removing the affected testicle is often the first treatment and, for some people, the only active treatment needed. Removing both testicles is not routine when only one is affected. Surgery to abdominal lymph nodes or other sites is reserved for particular situations rather than being automatic for everyone.

After surgery, one option may be surveillance: scheduled appointments, marker tests and scans to detect a recurrence early. This is an organized follow-up plan, not simply doing nothing. Other people need additional treatment to lower recurrence risk or treat known spread. Ask what the proposed approach is intended to achieve and what follow-up it requires.

Radiotherapy and chemotherapy have different roles

Radiotherapy uses targeted high-energy radiation. For testicular cancer it is generally external-beam treatment, with a machine directing radiation toward a selected area. It can be an option for some pure seminomas, particularly involving certain abdominal lymph nodes. Internal radioactive seeds are not a standard seminoma treatment.

Radiation is used less often for stage I seminoma now because surveillance or selected chemotherapy can avoid some long-term risks. Nonseminomas generally respond poorly to radiation, although it can have a role for selected metastases or symptom control. The tumor type and location matter.

Chemotherapy circulates through the body and can treat cancer cells beyond the testicle. Testicular-cancer regimens are commonly given through a vein, sometimes after surgery and sometimes for cancer that has spread or returned. The team explains the specific drugs, expected benefit and short- and long-term adverse effects. A general description of oral chemotherapy does not mean the usual regimen for this cancer is a course of tablets.

When high-dose treatment and stem-cell rescue are considered

Selected patients, often with cancer that has returned or has not responded sufficiently, may be offered high-dose chemotherapy with stem-cell support in a specialist service. It is not the automatic treatment for every advanced case.

The intensive chemotherapy can damage blood-forming cells as well as cancer cells. Stored stem cells are infused afterward to help rebuild blood-cell production. This support is different from a transplant directly attacking the tumor. Ask about the reason for the recommendation, alternatives and the monitoring needed during recovery.

Discuss fertility, hormones and recovery before treatment

Ask about sperm banking before treatment starts, even if having children is only a future possibility. Some treatment can reduce fertility temporarily or permanently. Removing one testicle does not necessarily cause infertility, because the remaining testicle may still function well; baseline fertility and any additional treatment also matter.

If both testicles need removal, sperm production is lost and hormone care also needs planning. A fertility specialist and the cancer team can explain what preservation options are feasible without delaying necessary care. Concerns about body image, sexual function or an artificial testicle are also valid topics for discussion.

The overall outlook is often favorable, especially for cancer found early, but a population survival percentage cannot predict one person’s outcome. Type, stage, marker levels and response to treatment all matter. Keep follow-up appointments after treatment and report new concerns rather than waiting for the next scheduled check.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Diagnosis combines examination, imaging, markers and pathology. Marker results alone cannot confirm or exclude every testicular cancer.

Treatment is selected by tumor type, stage and risk group. Surveillance, surgery, external radiotherapy and chemotherapy have different indications.

How BeMama can help

Bring questions about the pathology type, stage, treatment goal and sperm banking to the first specialist appointment. Ask who to contact if symptoms change while waiting.

When to seek help

Sudden severe testicular pain requires emergency care. For a lump, swelling or other lasting change, arrange prompt assessment even if there is no pain.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Get a new testicular change checked; cancer can be painless.
  • Ultrasound, blood markers and pathology answer different diagnostic questions.
  • Seminoma and nonseminoma do not have identical treatment plans.
  • Ask about sperm banking before treatment begins.
  • High treatability does not remove the need for follow-up or individualized advice.

Frequently asked questions

Can testicular cancer occur outside young adulthood?

Yes. It is often diagnosed in younger adults but can occur at other ages. Age alone should not determine whether a new change is checked.

Does a normal tumor-marker blood test rule it out?

No. Some tumors do not raise the measured markers. The team interprets results with examination, imaging and pathology.

Why might the whole testicle be removed instead of taking a small biopsy?

For a suspicious testicular mass, removal through the groin commonly provides the diagnosis and treats the primary tumor. A routine biopsy through the scrotum is usually avoided; selected exceptions require specialist judgment.

Will both testicles be removed?

Usually only the affected testicle is removed. Bilateral surgery is not routine and needs a specific reason.

Are radioactive seeds used for seminoma?

They are not standard treatment. When radiation is appropriate, testicular-cancer care generally uses an external beam targeted to a selected area.

Does every advanced case need a stem-cell transplant?

No. High-dose chemotherapy with stem-cell support is a specialist option for selected situations, often after relapse or insufficient response.

Can I have children after one testicle is removed?

Many people retain fertility, but cancer and additional treatment can affect it. Ask about sperm banking before treatment rather than relying on an assumption.

Is surveillance the same as being discharged without care?

No. It is a planned schedule of clinical checks, blood tests and imaging, with treatment if findings indicate recurrence.

When is testicular pain an emergency?

Sudden severe pain, particularly with nausea or vomiting, needs immediate assessment for problems such as torsion. Do not wait for a routine appointment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
